title: Azure Foundry Agent (Part 5)

# Foundry IQ: an agent that answers only from the documents Microsoft's learning path [Develop AI agents on Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/paths/develop-ai-agents-azure) includes a module on Foundry IQ, and its sample instructions look like a good template for any agent that must answer from documents. In this post I test that. I follow the module, use the six Minnesota traffic and car law documents from [Part 4](/posts/azurefoundryagent5/), and ask what the module's instructions change. I have built retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) several ways on this blog already, so I also compare this one with those at the end. ## What I found :::bullet-points - Foundry IQ gave me a working knowledge base over my documents in one script. The agent reached it as an MCP tool, and the answers came back with clickable sources. - The module's own code does not run as written. Its tool snippet fails with a 401 because it leaves out a project connection, and its `agent` call style is already deprecated. - Vague instructions ("use the knowledge base") still searched and cited. The difference showed up on questions the documents do not cover: the vague agent answered 3 of 6 of them with legal information the documents do not directly cover, and the strict agent answered none of them that way. - Strict rules have a cost. On one question the documents do answer, the strict agent said it had no information. - My results come from one run of 17 questions. They might be wrong. ::: ## What Foundry IQ is Foundry IQ is a managed knowledge layer on top of Azure AI Search. You put your documents in a search index, wrap the index in a **knowledge source**, and group sources into a **knowledge base**. The knowledge base then exposes one Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint with a single tool, `knowledge_base_retrieve`. Any agent can call that tool. ```mermaid flowchart LR D["6 law documents
80 sections"] --> I["Search index"] I --> S["Knowledge source"] S --> K["Knowledge base"] K --> M["MCP endpoint
knowledge_base_retrieve"] M --> A["Agent"] ``` The module's point is that retrieval is only half of the job. The agent's instructions decide whether it searches, whether it cites, and what it says when the answer is missing. ## Building it I created a new Foundry project, a model deployment and a search service, because my earlier Azure resources no longer existed. Everything sat in one resource group, so I could delete it afterwards. | Piece | What I used | |---|---| | Foundry account and project | `haddley-fiq-demo` and `fiq-demo`, in East US 2 | | Chat model | `gpt-5.4-mini`, capacity 100 | | Search service | Basic tier, in East US (East US 2 had no capacity for it) | Permissions took more work than anything else. I ran these role assignments myself, because my own tooling does not make them: | Who | Role | On | |---|---|---| | Me | Search Service Contributor and Search Index Data Contributor | The search service | | Me | Foundry Project Manager | The Foundry account | | The search service's identity | Cognitive Services User | The Foundry account, so the knowledge base can call the model | | The project's identity | Search Index Data Reader | The search service, so the agent can read the knowledge base | Then one script did the rest. It split each document at its `##` headings, which gave 80 sections, uploaded them as the search index, and created the knowledge source and the knowledge base. The knowledge base returns the matching passages ("extractive data"), uses `gpt-5.4-mini` for query planning, and has the retrieval reasoning effort set to low. ![](assets/images/azurefoundryagent6/knowledge-base.jpg) *I opened mn-law-kb in the portal and saw the model, the output mode and the knowledge source mn-law-ks, all Active* A quick direct test asked "Can I be charged with DWI if I am asleep in my parked car?" and the knowledge base returned the section on what counts as physical control, with the two cases that decide it. ## Where the module's code did not work :::watch-it The module's snippet fails in two ways **First, a 401.** The module creates the tool with only a server label and a server address. When I ran an agent built that way, the service replied that authentication to the MCP server failed with a 401. Microsoft's separate how-to article adds the missing piece: a project connection, of category `RemoteTool`, that signs in with the project's managed identity, and the tool then names that connection. **Second, a deprecated call.** The module calls the agent with `extra_body={"agent": ...}`. The service now rejects that and asks for `agent_reference`. Neither is a big problem, and both are easy to fix. They show how quickly the preview moves, so check the how-to article beside the module. ::: ## Four agents, one question set I built four agents on the same model and the same knowledge base, and I changed only the instructions and the connection. ![](assets/images/azurefoundryagent6/agents-list.jpg) *I saw all four agents Running in the portal: fiq-memory, fiq-snippet, fiq-vague and fiq-strict* The first has no knowledge base at all: ```text You answer questions about Minnesota traffic and car law. ``` The second is the module's own snippet, with no connection, so it fails. The third is the vague version: ```text You answer questions about Minnesota traffic and car law using the knowledge base. ``` The fourth follows the module's pattern: when to search, how to cite, and what to say when the answer is missing. ```text You are an assistant that gives general legal information about Minnesota traffic and car law. CRITICAL RULES: - You must ALWAYS search the knowledge base before answering any question. - You must NEVER answer from your own knowledge or training data. - Every answer must name the document section it came from, in this format: [Document: section title]. - If the knowledge base does not contain the answer, respond with exact …(truncated)
